disclaimer.heading: Before you use this
disclaimer.body:
This app exists because the other ones answer every question. It will often tell you that it cannot identify what you have photographed, and that is the app working, not failing.

It will never tell you that a mushroom is safe to eat. No app can. People are killed every year by mushrooms that were identified confidently and wrongly, and the species responsible have ordinary lookalikes that experienced foragers collect on purpose.

acknowledgements.statement: I understand this app will never tell me a mushroom is safe to eat.
acknowledgements.because: There is no such category in it. It names what it can and warns about recorded hazards. Where there is no hazard on record it says nothing at all, which is not the same as saying it is safe.

acknowledgements.statement: I understand a photograph cannot rule out a deadly lookalike.
acknowledgements.because: The features that separate the dangerous species from their ordinary lookalikes are usually underground, underneath, or only visible hours later in a spore print.

acknowledgements.statement: I will not eat a wild mushroom on the strength of what this app tells me.
acknowledgements.because: An identification here is a starting point for a person who already knows what they are doing, and nothing more than that.

acknowledgements.statement: I understand this build has no trained model, and the identifications it produces are placeholders.
acknowledgements.because: The classifier has not been trained yet. Results come from a stub that produces consistent but meaningless answers, so that everything around it can be built and tested.

acknowledgements.statement: I understand the percentages shown are not probabilities.
acknowledgements.because: Calibration has not been fitted. Until it is, a number is an ordering between candidates and nothing more -- 80% does not mean eight times in ten.

acknowledgements.statement: I understand the reference data has not been checked by a mycologist.
acknowledgements.because: Which species are dangerous, which are confused with which, and what separates them are compiled from standard references and have not been reviewed by a qualified person. Errors in that data become errors in every answer.

fields.label: Surroundings
fields.prompt: What trees are within about ten metres?
fields.how: Many fungi partner with one kind of tree and grow nowhere else, so this narrows the possibilities sharply.

fields.label: What it is growing on
fields.prompt: What is it growing on or out of?
fields.how: Look at what the base actually emerges from, not just what is nearby. Buried wood and roots count as wood.

fields.label: Growth habit
fields.how: Step back and photograph the whole group in place.

fields.label: Cap colour
fields.how: Photograph from above in natural light, avoiding deep shade.

fields.label: Gill colour
fields.prompt: What colour are the gills right now?
fields.how: Describe the colour of the gills themselves, not the cap.

fields.label: Ring on the stem
fields.prompt: Is there a ring or skirt of tissue on the stem?
fields.how: Look partway up the stem for a collar, skirt or a distinct zone of fibres.

fields.label: Smell
fields.how: Break a piece and smell it immediately, close up.

fields.label: Spore print
fields.prompt: What colour is the spore print?
fields.how: Cut the cap off and lay it gills-down on paper that is half white and half black, cover it with a bowl, and leave it for two to twelve hours. The colour of the powder that falls is the spore print.

field_form.note: Every field is optional. Answer only what you actually observed -- a guess is worse than a blank, because the app cannot tell the two apart.

result.headline: This doesn't match anything I know well
result.detail: The photograph does not resemble any species in my range with reasonable confidence. It may be a species I was never trained on, or the photograph may not show enough of the mushroom.
warnings: Because this does not match anything I know, I cannot tell you what it is -- and I cannot rule out that it is one of the species that can kill. Treat an unidentified mushroom as more dangerous than a named one, not less.

questions.label: Bruising
questions.prompt: Does it change colour when cut or rubbed?
questions.how: Cut the mushroom in half lengthways, including the very base of the stem, and rub the cap edge. Wait a full two minutes and watch for a change.
options: Yellow, especially at the stem base
questions.safety_note: Chrome-yellow staining at the base of the stem marks the Yellow Stainer, the commonest cause of mushroom poisoning in Britain.
questions.rationale: This separates Amanita virosa, which can kill, from Amanita pantherina.

questions.label: Ring on the stem
questions.prompt: Is there a ring or skirt of tissue on the stem?
questions.how: Look partway up the stem for a collar, skirt or a distinct zone of fibres.
questions.rationale: This separates Amanita virosa, which can kill, from Amanita pantherina.

questions.label: Base of the stem
questions.prompt: Dig up the very base of the stem. Is there a cup or bag around it?
questions.how: Do not cut the mushroom at ground level. Lever the whole thing out with a knife or your fingers so the base comes up intact, then brush off the soil. You are looking for a sac, cup or rim of tissue around the bottom.
questions.safety_note: This is the single most important check in mushroom foraging. The sac at the base is the mark of Amanita, the genus responsible for most fatal poisonings. It is often buried and is routinely cut off and missed.
questions.rationale: This separates Amanita virosa, which can kill, from Amanita pantherina.

result.headline: Most likely Tricholoma saponaceum
result.detail: Smells of household soap, and the flesh in the stem base turns pink or reddish when cut. Colour is unreliable -- grey, olive, brownish or nearly white on different collections.

questions.how: Cut the cap off and lay it gills-down on paper that is half white and half black, cover it with a bowl, and leave it for two to twelve hours. The colour of the powder that falls is the spore print.
questions.rationale: This is what separates Tricholoma pardinum from Coprinopsis lagopus.
